subject: research/qual-induce
professional: a computational social scientist or NLP researcher who has refereed papers on topic-model evaluation and annotation-scheme agreement. They would check first that the held-out protocol has no leakage, that agreement is chance-corrected, that a coverage number has a null baseline, and whether the result is new against prior topic-model-vs-label work.

evidence.correctness: I fetched the GoEmotions CSV (curl to storage.googleapis.com, 14,174,600 bytes) and wrote scratchpad indep.py, which does NOT import qualinduce.py: own csv loader, own primary-label rule, own NMI (arithmetic-mean normaliser, from counts), own rank-based AUC (scipy rankdata) and a chance estimate from 20 permutations. Results vs README: (1) corpus n=5313 and 1906 comments with a unique majority primary emotion: exact match. (2) Per-emotion positive counts give exactly the 15 evaluable emotions at seed 0 and the unmeasured ones the README names (grief 4, relief 8, nervousness 8, pride 11): match. (3) Seed-0 split, NMF k=10 held-out NMI 0.163 (README mean over 5 splits 0.161), chance 0.055 (README 0.058); k=27 NMI 0.263 (README 0.258), chance 0.118 (README 0.120). (4) Seed-0 best-code AUC, 15 emotions: k=10 mean 0.617, share>=0.7 0.27; k=27 mean 0.630 (README means over 5 seeds 0.603 and 0.616, share>=0.7 0.21 and 0.22): consistent with seed variation. I also reran the full experiments/run.py (7m46s wall, user 14m55s; README says about 1.5 minutes). All NMF rows reproduced to the printed precision. Four k-means rows did not: stability k=5 0.486 vs committed 0.471, k=10 0.395 vs 0.380, share>=0.6 at k=10 0.30 vs 0.35, pairs above 0.3 at k=5 0.140 vs 0.100 (diff against a saved copy of results.txt; I restored results.txt with git checkout afterwards). The k-means numbers drift by up to 0.05 between runs, so they are not exactly reproducible on this sklearn 1.9.1 / numpy 2.4.6. The numbers that exist are right; the qualitative picture is unchanged.
evidence.completeness: Claimed items checked. (a) Unit tests: `cd research/qual-induce && python3 -m unittest test_qualinduce` ran 7, OK, 0.4 s. (b) Reproduce script experiments/run.py: ran to completion and rewrote results.txt (see correctness). (c) results.txt tables match the README tables (read side by side). (d) All four measures (agreement, coverage, redundancy, stability) exist and run for 2 methods x 4 k x 5 splits. (e) Example top-word lists in the README match results.txt for NMF. (f) experiments/figure.py and the live page https://marisstella.app/research/qual-induce/ were not run or loaded by me. (g) The stated next steps (LLM-proposed codebook, human-vs-human ceiling, topical corpus) are honestly marked as not done. No TODOs or stubs found in qualinduce.py or run.py. Everything it claims to do works; the scope is a no-LLM baseline.
evidence.verification: Test command: `python3 -m unittest test_qualinduce`, 7 tests, OK. Three hand-seeded mutations in qualinduce.py, each reverted by restoring a saved copy (git status clean afterwards). (1) nmi_vs_label `keep = label >= 0` -> `label >= -1` (admits the 'no unique primary' items into NMI, the sample definition behind every NMI number): NOT caught, 7 OK. (2) coverage(): choose the best code on the held-out half instead of the training half (`roc_auc_score(H_train,S_train)` -> `H_test,S_test`, i.e. the exact leakage the README says it avoids): NOT caught, 7 OK, because the test passes identical train and test matrices. (3) coverage(): `argmax` -> `argmin` of the training AUCs: caught (1 failure). So 1 of 3. The tests are synthetic planted-topic checks (three duplicated sentences) plus tiny unit checks. Nothing tests load(), the rater-majority filter on a real file, the train/test separation, the chance permutation inside the pipeline, or run.py. Reading and running only the tests would suggest more protection than exists.
evidence.craft: Read qualinduce.py (about 150 lines), experiments/run.py, test_qualinduce.py, project.json. The module is small, documented and readable, and uses a train/test split sensibly. Defects: (1) run.py's stability measure fits cb2 on the held-out half `tb` and then applies it to `tb`, so cb2 is scored on its own training data (run.py, the `cb2 = qi.Codebook(m, k, seed + 100).fit(tb)` line); (2) run.py calls `main()` at module level with no `if __name__ == '__main__'` guard and defines `defaultdict_list` below its use site; (3) redundancy(S_b) is computed twice per cell; (4) no requirements.txt or pinned versions, and k-means rows drift between runs (see correctness); (5) the chance NMI is one permutation per split drawn from a shared RandomState, so it is itself noisy and order-dependent; (6) Codebook.fit for k-means builds `words` with a Python loop over clusters, and an empty cluster silently gets a zero vector; (7) the human row of the redundancy table is computed in run.py but the 'AUC 1 by construction' comment leaves a dangling stub comment. No silent network failure: fetch() raises.
evidence.claims: Backed: corpus counts 5,313 and 1,906; NMI 0.258 vs 0.120 (k=27) and 0.341 vs 0.195 (k=60), mean |r| of NMF 0.016 to 0.039, k-means k=5/10 redundancy 10 to 12 percent (as committed; my rerun gave 14 percent and 11.6 percent), best-code AUC about 0.6, at most a quarter reaching 0.7, 12 unevaluable emotions, 'not an LLM' limitation, all correct against results.txt. Not backed: (1) The lede says 'The excess over chance is 0.10 to 0.15 at every size'. From results.txt the excess is NMF 0.072 (k=5), 0.103 (10), 0.138 (27), 0.146 (60) and k-means 0.043, 0.093, 0.118, 0.135, so it is below 0.10 at k=5 for both methods and at k=10 for k-means. (2) 'Reading the numbers' says 'the excess over chance is roughly flat'; the same table shows it rising with k (0.07 to 0.15 for NMF, 0.04 to 0.14 for k-means). The conclusion that raw NMI flatters large k still holds, but the flat-excess description is wrong. (3) The stability column is described as NMI 'between two codebooks induced on disjoint halves and applied to the same held-out comments'; one of the two codebooks was induced on those very comments (craft defect 1), so the column is inflated. (4) 'about 1.5 minutes' runtime: measured 7m46s. (5) 'Weakly ... only a little above chance' is a verdict with no human-vs-human ceiling or coverage null to compare against, though the README says so itself in Next steps. Disclaimers: produced-with-AI note present, limitations section honest.
evidence.fitness: Research bar: PhD-level programme aimed at a publishable result (research/CLAUDE.md, PROJECTS.md track qual, milestone 4). A researcher could reuse the Codebook class and the four measures, and the honest chance baseline is the useful part. But it is one corpus, 1,906 NMI items (about 950 per half), two classical methods, and it is explicitly the baseline for an LLM comparison that has not been run, so no finding exists that a paper could rest on. Nearest prior work: Demszky et al. 2020 (GoEmotions, which already analyses the correlation structure of the emotions and uses PPCA on annotations); Chang et al. 2009 'Reading tea leaves' (topic-model fit does not track human judgement of topics); the long standing practice of scoring clusters with NMI against gold labels; and TopicGPT (Pham et al. 2024) and LLooM (Lam et al. 2024), which themselves compare against LDA, BERTopic or NMF-style baselines against human labels. Of these only the last two are cited. That NMF topics on short Reddit comments poorly separate emotions is expected, so the result is sound but not new; the new thing would be the LLM arm.
evidence.domain: Compared against standard cluster-evaluation and annotation-reliability practice. Matches: NMI against a gold label with a permutation chance floor, fit on one half and scored on the other, five splits with sd reported, and a rater-majority label rule shared with qual-real. Departs: (1) there is no chance baseline for the coverage AUC, although each reported AUC is the max over 5 to 60 codes (chosen on the training half, which removes leakage but not the positive bias of best-of-k selection); a permuted-label null would show how much of 0.60 to 0.62 is selection; (2) no human-vs-human ceiling, so 'weak' has no reference, and the 27 labels are rater-majority with only 3 to 5 raters, which is noisy; (3) the NMI uses only the 36 percent of comments with a unique majority primary emotion, a subset the README itself says is probably easier; (4) NMI with k=60 on about 950 items is strongly upward biased, so the chance column is the right control, but a chance-adjusted measure such as AMI or ARI would be the usual choice; (5) stability is in-sample for one codebook; (6) topic-style induction on short single-sentence comments is a known weak setting, and stopword removal and min_df=3 remove many affect words (not tested). A reviewer would accept the framing and ask for these before the LLM comparison.

defects.what: Stability metric compares a codebook induced on half A with one induced on half B, but scores both on half B, so the second codebook is evaluated on its own training data; the README describes the two as induced on disjoint halves and applied to held-out comments. The stability column is inflated.

README lede states the excess NMI over chance is 0.10 to 0.15 at every size, and the Reading section calls it roughly flat. results.txt gives 0.072 (NMF k=5), 0.043 (k-means k=5), 0.093 (k-means k=10), and a monotone rise with k.

Test suite does not guard the held-out protocol: seeding the coverage selection to use the held-out half, or widening the NMI sample to items without a primary label, both leave 7 of 7 tests passing (2 of 3 seeded mutations survived).
Coverage AUCs (best of 5 to 60 codes per emotion) have no permuted-label null, so the part of the 0.60 to 0.62 headline that is selection bias is unknown.

k-means rows are not reproducible: a rerun on sklearn 1.9.1 changed stability, redundancy share and AUC share by up to 0.05 (NMF rows reproduced exactly); no requirements file pins versions. README runtime of about 1.5 minutes measured 7m46s.
run.py executes main() at import with no __main__ guard, computes redundancy twice per cell, and the chance NMI is a single permutation per split.

verdict: A small, honestly framed no-LLM baseline whose numbers are real: I recomputed the corpus counts, the 15 evaluable emotions, held-out NMI and chance, and best-code AUCs with an independent implementation, and the committed NMF table reproduced exactly on a full rerun. It does not meet the bar because verification is weak (2 of 3 seeded mutations survive, including selecting the coverage code on the held-out half) and claims are not fully backed: the headline 'excess 0.10 to 0.15 at every size' and 'roughly flat' contradict its own table, and the stability column is in-sample for one codebook. It is finished for its stated scope (completeness 3) but not new: topic-versus-gold-label evaluation with NMI is standard, and the novel part, the LLM-proposed arm, is not done. Fixes are small (correct the README sentence, fit cb2 and score on a third half, add a permuted-label null for coverage, add protocol tests).
